title: Liguria's Metano Price Has Climbed Nearly 40% Since Summer, Far Outpacing the Rest of Italy
dek: Benzina and Gasolio are easing off their September highs in Liguria, but the region's gas-based fuels are telling a sharply different story.
executive_summary: As of October 16, 2026, Liguria's self-service pump prices sit at €2.0352/L for Benzina, €2.2681/L for Gasolio, €0.894/L for GPL and €1.989/kg for Metano, broadly flat against the prior reading on October 13 (Benzina -0.22%, Gasolio -0.07%, GPL and Metano unchanged). Against the national same-day average, Liguria undercuts the rest of Italy on both liquid fuels — Benzina by 0.48% and Gasolio by 0.43% — while running noticeably hotter on its two gas-based fuels, with GPL sitting 15.2% above the national average and Metano 5.4% above it. The region's 539 registered stations reported at a 91.3% rate today, a touch ahead of the 90.4% national reporting rate.

Those same-day numbers undersell what has actually happened in Liguria since tracking began on July 21. The region's Metano price has climbed roughly 39% from €1.429/kg in the week of July 20 to €1.989/kg in the week of October 12 — outpacing the national Metano rise of about 25% over the identical twelve weeks, and making it by a wide margin the most volatile fuel in the region this autumn. GPL has moved in a similarly lopsided way, up about 7.5% in Liguria since week 30 while the national GPL average has barely moved (+2%). Benzina and Gasolio, by contrast, both rode a wave up through late September and have since pulled back by comparable amounts in Liguria and nationally — suggesting Liguria's real divergence from the rest of Italy isn't at the pump for cars, but in its LPG and natural-gas network.

fuel_sections.heading: Benzina Eases Off Its September Peak, Still a Touch Cheaper Than the Rest of Italy
paragraphs: Liguria's self-service Benzina price stood at €2.0352/L on October 16, down €0.0044 (-0.22%) from the €2.0396/L recorded on October 13. That keeps the region 0.48% below the national same-day average of €2.0451/L, continuing a pattern seen through most of the tracked period in which Liguria's Benzina price has sat at or just under the Italian average.

Zoomed out, Liguria's weekly Benzina average traced the same rough arc as the rest of the country: from €1.9885/L in the week of July 20 (week 30) it climbed almost continuously to a peak of €2.1802/L in the week of September 21 (week 39) — a rise of 9.6% — before falling back to €2.0374/L by the week of October 12 (week 42), a pullback of 6.6% from the peak. Nationally, the same period saw a nearly identical climb (+9.7% trough-to-peak) but a slightly gentler retreat (-5.6%), meaning Liguria's recent Benzina relief has actually been a little sharper than the rest of Italy's.

fuel_sections.heading: Gasolio Pulls Back From Its Late-September High, Tracking a Touch Below the National Line
paragraphs: Gasolio self-service in Liguria priced at €2.2681/L on October 16, essentially flat against the €2.2698/L seen on October 13 (-0.07%), and 0.43% cheaper than the national same-day average of €2.278/L.

The multi-week picture shows Gasolio bottoming out at €2.1147/L in the week of August 10 (week 33) before surging to €2.3865/L by the week of September 21 (week 39) — a 12.9% climb — then easing back to €2.269/L by week 42, a 4.9% retreat from the high. Nationally, Gasolio followed an almost parallel path (+12.3% trough-to-peak, -4.1% since), so Liguria's diesel market has moved in lockstep with the rest of Italy, if anything pulling back slightly harder from its September spike.

fuel_sections.heading: GPL Is Liguria's Biggest Outlier — Up 7.5% Since July While the National Average Barely Moves
paragraphs: GPL held steady at €0.894/L in Liguria on both October 13 and October 16 — no day-over-day move — but that price sits 15.2% above the national same-day average of €0.7758/L, the widest fuel gap between Liguria and the rest of Italy in today's data.

That gap has been building all autumn. Liguria's weekly GPL average has moved unusually for a single region: €0.832/L in week 30, a jump to €0.884/L by week 35 (a premium that held through most of August), a pullback to €0.8383/L by weeks 38-39, and then a renewed climb to €0.894/L by weeks 41-42 — a net rise of about 7.5% since tracking began. The national GPL average, by contrast, has been essentially flat across the same twelve weeks, inching from €0.7592/L to €0.7745/L, a rise of roughly 2%. Liguria's LPG market is not just pricier than the rest of the country — on these tracked weeks, it has been getting pricier at more than three times the national pace.

fuel_sections.heading: Metano Has Risen Nearly 40% Since Summer in Liguria — The Region's Sharpest Move of the Season
paragraphs: Metano priced at €1.989/kg in Liguria on October 16, unchanged from October 13, but running 5.4% above the national same-day average of €1.8871/kg.

No fuel in this region has moved as much this season. Liguria's weekly Metano average has risen in almost every tracked week, from €1.429/kg in week 30 to €1.989/kg by weeks 41-42 — a 39.2% increase over twelve weeks. The national Metano average rose too, but by notably less: from €1.4999/kg to €1.8796/kg, a 25.3% increase over the same stretch. Liguria's Metano price has grown at roughly 1.5 times the national rate since late July, the single most pronounced regional-vs-national divergence in this report.

network_section.heading: 492 of 539 Stations Reporting — A Strong 91% Coverage Rate
paragraphs: Liguria's registry lists 539 fuel stations, of which 492 reported at least one price on October 16 — a 91.3% reporting rate.

That is slightly ahead of the national reporting rate of 90.4% (21,639 of 23,928 registered stations reporting today), suggesting Liguria's price feed is marginally more complete than the Italian average on any given day — useful context for reading the regional comparisons above as representative of the market rather than a thin sample.

methodology_section.heading: How This Report Gets Made — Without a Spreadsheet in Sight
paragraphs: Every figure, trend comparison and sentence in this report — the daily price pull, the weekly trend math, which region gets featured today, and the prose itself — is produced automatically by an unattended pipeline built with Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent. No analyst opens a spreadsheet each morning to re-key MIMIT's price feed, recompute week-over-week averages, or decide which region's story is worth telling; the pipeline does all of it, every day, without manual intervention.

That is a meaningfully different approach from a manually-maintained Excel tracker, where updating even a single day's regional comparison would mean re-pasting CSVs, rebuilding pivot tables, and writing the commentary by hand. Automating the whole chain — ingestion, analysis, writing and publishing — means the report can go deeper (full weekly trend lines, cross-fuel comparisons, a different region every day) at effectively zero marginal effort, something a hand-updated spreadsheet could never sustain daily.

pull_quote: Liguria's Metano price has climbed nearly 39% since late July — about one and a half times the national rate of increase.
caption:
Today's Fuel Dashboard spotlight: Liguria.

Self-service Benzina and Gasolio in Liguria are both running slightly below the national average right now (-0.5% and -0.4%), but the real story this week is gas. Liguria's Metano price has climbed almost 39% since late July, well ahead of the roughly 25% rise seen nationally over the same twelve weeks, and GPL has pulled 15% above the national average too, rising more than three times as fast as the rest of Italy since tracking began.

Fuel Dashboard is a live, self-updating site that pulls Italy's official MIMIT fuel price feed every day, picks a region to spotlight, computes the week-over-week trends, and writes up the findings, all automatically. No spreadsheet, no manual pivot tables, no analyst re-pasting CSVs each morning: the whole pipeline, including this write-up, runs on Claude Code.

That's the real pitch here: a one-person side project can now ship something that would have taken a small analytics team to maintain as a manual Excel tracker, not because the data is secret, but because AI tools make daily ingestion, analysis and writing cheap enough to automate end to end.
